hints: Notice the diagram gives both a $60\text{ m}$ slope length and a $30\text{ m}$ vertical height, so the $0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}$ along the escalator is not the vertical speed.
Recall power for lifting at constant speed is $P = Fv$ with $F$ equal to weight and $v$ the vertical component of velocity.
Calculate the vertical speed from the $30/60$ ratio, then find $mgv$ for $20 \times 60\text{ kg}$ and add the constant $2.0\text{ kW}$ for friction.
walkthrough: Total passenger mass is $m = 20 \times 60\text{ kg} = 1200\text{ kg}$, with weight $W = mg$.
The escalator speed $0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is along the $60\text{ m}$ slope, while gravity acts through the $30\text{ m}$ vertical height.
Vertical component of velocity is $v_v = 0.75\text{ m s}^{-1} \times 30/60 = 0.375\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Power to lift passengers is rate of gain of potential energy: $P_{lift} = mgv_v = 1200 \times 9.81 \times 0.375 \approx 4415\text{ W} \approx 4.4\text{ kW}$.
Add the constant friction power: $P_{total} = 4.4\text{ kW} + 2.0\text{ kW} = 6.4\text{ kW}$. This is option B.

options.A: This is only the power to lift the passengers at $0.375\text{ m s}^{-1}$ vertically. It omits the constant $2.0\text{ kW}$ needed to overcome friction.
options.B: The sum of $2.0\text{ kW}$ for friction and about $4.4\text{ kW}$ to gain gravitational potential energy gives about $6.4\text{ kW}$.
options.C: This uses the $0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}$ slope speed as if it were the vertical speed, so it doubles the lifting power and also omits friction.
options.D: This uses the $0.75\text{ m s}^{-1}$ slope speed as the vertical speed to get about $8.8\text{ kW}$, then adds $2.0\text{ kW}$ for friction.
